title: Using Secrets in Workflows knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Using Secrets in Workflows?
options: Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
Pass secrets only to the steps that need them through environment variables or action inputs, never print them, and remember masking cannot prevent every leak.
questions.answer_key: Pass secrets only to the steps that need them through environment variables or action inputs, never print them, and remember masking cannot prevent every leak.
questions.explanation: This is the central behavior of using secrets in workflows: Pass secrets only to the steps that need them through environment variables or action inputs, never print them, and remember masking cannot prevent every leak. Validate configuration and behavior against the current official reference before production use.

questions.answer_key: Store credentials in the appropriate protected secret store, pass them only to the step that needs them, and never print or save them in logs, summaries, artifacts, or caches.

questions.prompt: How should a reviewer verify a change related to using secrets in workflows?
options: Assume the workflow is correct as soon as the YAML file is committed.
Retry every failure without looking at the exit code or preserving evidence.
Publish the workflow to production before reviewing its triggers and permissions.
Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
questions.answer_key: Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Reliable verification uses observable evidence. For this lesson, consider: Pass secrets only to the steps that need them through environment variables or action inputs, never print them, and remember masking cannot prevent every leak. A syntax check alone cannot prove remote execution, permissions, or deployment behavior.
